say: In 1983, builders in Gwahng-joe, in southern China, struck a sealed stone tomb. It belonged to a king of Nahn-yweh, a lost kingdom claimed by both Chinese and Vietnamese history.
He lay in a suit of more than two thousand jade plates, sewn together with silk thread.
On his body lay a gold seal with a coiled dragon. Its inscription reads: seal of Emperor Wen.
But the Han histories call this man a king, King Wen of Nahn-yweh. A king in the books. An emperor in his own tomb.
His grandfather, Jow Twaw, was a Chin officer from the north. Vietnam's first national chronicle made him an emperor of its own. Later Vietnamese historians called him an invader.
So whose kingdom was Nahn-yweh? Let's look at what the sources actually say.
Around 214 BC, armies of the Chin, the first Chinese empire, pushed south across the mountains.
Chin set up three new commanderies there: Nahn-hye, Gway-lin and Shyahng.
Convicts and settlers were sent to live among the local peoples, whom the Chinese called the Yweh.
One of the northern officers was Jow Twaw, from Jun-ding in the north. Chin made him magistrate of Long-chwahn, a county of Nahn-hye.
Then rebellions broke out in the north. The dying commander of Nahn-hye, Ren Shyow, called Jow Twaw to his bed.
According to Suh-mah Chyen, Ren told him that Pahn-yoo, guarded by mountains and the sea, could be the heart of a state.
Jow Twaw took command. He closed the mountain passes, cut the new roads, and replaced Chin officials with his own men.
When Chin collapsed, he took Gway-lin and Shyahng as well, and around 204 BC named himself King of Nahn-yweh. His capital was Pahn-yoo, today's Gwahng-joe.
Who were the Yweh? Not one nation. Chinese writers used the word for many southern peoples, the Hundred Yweh.
Chinese texts describe Yweh people who cut their hair short and tattooed their bodies.
In 196 BC, the new Han emperor sent an envoy south: Loo Jyah.
Suh-mah Chyen says Jow Twaw received him with his hair in a southern bun, sprawling with his legs stretched out.
Loo Jyah scolded him. You are a man of the Central States, he said. Your family graves are in the north.
Jow Twaw sat up. I have lived among the southern peoples so long, he said, that I have forgotten my manners.
Then he laughed. I did not rise up in China, he said, so I am king here. Had I been there, why would I be any less than the Han?
His court mixed northern settlers with Yweh nobles. And Suh-mah Chyen lists Pahn-yoo as a rich market for pearls and rhinoceros horn.
Loo Jyah gave him a Han seal as King of Nahn-yweh, and Jow Twaw agreed to serve Han as a vassal.
Then, under Empress Lyoo, Han officials banned the sale of iron goods to Nahn-yweh at the border markets.
Jow Twaw blamed the neighbouring king of Chahng-shah. He declared himself Emperor of Nahn-yweh and attacked Chahng-shah's border towns.
Han sent an army. Heat and disease stopped it at the mountains. When the empress died, in 180 BC, the war ended.
Han records say Jow Twaw then used his army and his wealth to bring neighbours under his sway, including the Western Oh and the Lwaw.
In 179 BC, the new emperor Wen repaired Jow Twaw's family graves in the north, and sent Loo Jyah south again.
Jow Twaw wrote back as your old servant, great chief of the barbarians. He had called himself emperor, he wrote, only to amuse himself.
But Suh-mah Chyen adds a quiet line. Inside his own kingdom, Jow Twaw kept the old title. A king to Han. An emperor at home.
Decades later, his grandson was buried with a seal that said exactly that. Emperor.
What about the Red River, in today's northern Vietnam? Here, two kinds of record tell different stories.
For this region, the Han histories only name the Western Oh and the Lwaw, won over with gifts and the threat of an army.
Many historians connect the Lwaw with the Lahk of the Red River plains.
Vietnamese tradition tells a story instead, written down many centuries later.
The legend says King Ahn Zuong of Oh Lahk built a spiral citadel at Koh Lwah. A golden turtle gave him a claw, to make the trigger of a magic crossbow.
With it he could not be beaten. So Jow Twaw made peace, the story goes, and sent his son Chong Twee to marry the king's daughter, Mee Chow.
Chong Twee secretly swapped the claw, then went home. Jow Twaw attacked, and the crossbow failed.
The king fled with Mee Chow, who left goose feathers for her husband to follow. At the sea, the turtle named her the enemy, and the king killed her.
Even the date is disputed: around 208 BC in the Vietnamese chronicle, around 180 BC in many modern accounts.
Archaeology adds something else. Koh Lwah is real: huge earthen walls, the oldest layers from around 300 BC.
Digs found bronze arrowheads, and stone moulds to cast them. That shows a strong local power. It does not prove the legend.
Most historians think Nahn-yweh ruled the Red River through local lords.
Jow Twaw died in 137 BC. The Vietnamese chronicle says he lived to a hundred and twenty-one, a number we cannot check.
His grandson took the throne, the king from the tomb. The histories call him Jow Hoo. His own seal says Jow Maw.
When Han asked him to come to court, his ministers warned: go, and you will never come back. He stayed home, pleading illness.
His son Ying-chee, Suh-mah Chyen says, hid away the old seal of Jow Twaw. The one that said Emperor.
Ying-chee had married a woman from Hahn-dahn, in the north. Their young son became king, and she became queen mother.
Han envoys came again. One, Suh-mah Chyen says, had once been her lover.
The queen mother and the young king asked to join Han, under Han law.
The minister Lyoo Jyah, trusted by the Yweh, refused. He told the kingdom the queen was a woman of the Central States, ready to hand its treasures to Han.
In 112 BC, he killed the king, the queen mother and the Han envoys, and put another prince on the throne.
Emperor Wu sent armies and river fleets south. In the winter of 111 BC, Pahn-yoo burned and surrendered.
Nahn-yweh became nine Han commanderies. Three of them, Jyow-jir, Jyoh-jun and Ree-nahn, lay in what is now northern and north-central Vietnam.
Five generations, ninety-three years, Suh-mah Chyen counts. Then the kingdom was gone.
So whose kingdom was it? Each side has its own answer, and the answers have changed over time.
To Suh-mah Chyen, Nahn-yweh's kings were Han vassals, and 111 BC meant the Yweh lands were finally settled.
In Vietnam, the story began differently. In 1272, Lay Vahn Hew wrote the first national chronicle, and began it with Jow Twaw, as Chee-oh Voo Day.
He praised him for opening up our Vee-et land and standing up to the Han.
In the eighteenth century, the scholar Ngoh Tee See disagreed. Jow Twaw ruled from Pahn-yoo, he argued, as a foreign king.
Many twentieth-century Vietnamese historians followed that line. Jow Twaw became an invader, and King Ahn Zuong the ruler who lost to him.
In Gwahng-joe, the tomb is now a museum, and Nahn-yweh is presented as the region's own heritage, the culture of Ling-nahn.
Modern historians, like Keith Taylor and Erica Brindley, point to a problem with all of these answers.
Around 200 BC, there was no China or Vietnam as we know them. Yweh was an outsider's word for many peoples, and Nahn-yweh was a mixed kingdom.
A northern family ruled it, through southern lords. Later nations each read their own story into it.
Nahn-yweh did not quite disappear. Its name came back, two thousand years later.
In the early 1800s, the new Nwin ruler Zah Long asked the Ching court to recognise his kingdom as Nahm Vee-et.
Ching records show the court objected. Ancient Nahn-yweh had covered Gwahng-dong and Gwahng-shee, lands now part of the Ching.
So in 1804 the two words were turned around. The country became Vee-et Nahm.
A Nahn-yweh king's jade suit now lies in a Gwahng-joe museum. And the name of his lost kingdom lives on, reversed, in the name of a country.
Was Nahn-yweh Chinese, Vietnamese, or neither? Tell us what you think in the comments, and subscribe to Rice and Empires.
